value.text: Residents of West Palm Beach's Riverwalk community say they have been trapped for days by floodwaters left behind after a one-in-1,000-year rain event, with streets nearly impassable and residents reporting fish, venomous snakes and even alligators outside their homes.Several residents reached out to WPTV asking for help as the water lingered throughout the neighborhood.When WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman entered RiverWalk, he found flooded streets, residents unable to go about their normal routines, and at least one alligator swimming near a home."It's like an apocalyptic-type event," resident Don Gentile told Hoffman.Resident Bobbi Jo Morgan said the flooding is unlike anything she has experienced in the neighborhood."This is nothing that we've seen before," Morgan said.Residents told Hoffman every street in the community had experienced some level of flooding.Gentile said residents were hoping the water would eventually recede from the roadways."Hopefully this will dissipate in the roadways," Gentile said. "But every street in this community has some kind of flooding on it."The floodwaters have also brought an unusual concern directly to residents' homes.Residents told Hoffman they had spotted fish and venomous snakes in the flooded streets.Then, while Gentile was walking Hoffman into his backyard, they came face to face with an alligator in the water."What was that?" Gentile asked."That was an alligator," Hoffman responded.Gentile's neighbor, James Whited, was stunned by its size."That thing had to be — his head was bigger than a Volkswagen," Whited said.The encounter illustrated another challenge residents are facing as floodwater remains throughout the community: Wildlife can now move through areas normally occupied by people.For some families, the flooding has disrupted more than their ability to drive through the neighborhood.Some children have been unable to get to school."I think the office main area got flooded, and that's the only thing that is stopping me from going to school," young Blake Zeitz told Hoffman.Residents said the neighborhood association has been working to develop a plan, but they fear the standing water could remain for days or even weeks.Hoffman found it difficult to enter the neighborhood, with portions of the roadway nearly impassable because of the water.Residents also told Hoffman that Amazon deliveries were no longer reaching parts of the community.Some people were purchasing plane tickets and planning to leave the area until conditions improve, according to residents. Others said they had little choice but to remain in their homes and wait for the water to recede.As the water lingers, some residents are questioning what preparations could have been made for an extreme rainfall event and what can be done when flooding reaches this level.Debra Zeitz questioned why there was not an emergency response capable of addressing the neighborhood's situation."We're Palm Beach County. We're known for hurricanes and water and rain," Zeitz said. "Why can't they predict something like this, too, or at least set up some kind of emergency way to deal with that?"For Riverwalk residents, the immediate problem remains right outside their doors: flooded streets, disrupted daily life and uncertainty about when their neighborhood will finally dry out.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community as dangerous waters continue to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. I think it's part of living in Florida," said Sheri George, a Vitalia resident. Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission on a swamp buggy Wednesday. They had no electricity, no A/C and the food in their refrigerator was spoiling. They were unable to drive out of the neighborhood because roads were flooded. They were thrilled FWC could get them safely out of the neighborhood. This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer," Sheri George said. "I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me," said Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident who was evacuated because of flooding. According to FWC, since Tuesday they've evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater in several areas in St. "I love being able to, when we're at our worst times being able to come and give somebody some ray of hope," said Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator who was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. "I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety," said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer. Lucie Police Department said officers and emergency personnel were helping residents affected by ongoing flooding get to safety. The department urged people to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents told CBS12 they were effectively trapped in their homes and unable to get their cars out of their driveways because of flooded streets. Some said water reached their garages but did not enter their homes. CBS12 also observed water 18 inches deep in the street. See also: Two injured, third person believed dead after helicopter crash near Key Biscayne The flooding has continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. Lucie received 16.7 inches of rain from Nov. Lucie County received between 7 and 17 inches during that period, according to the National Weather Service. Residents told CBS12 the flooding was the worst they had seen in their neighborhood. Police urged residents to never drive or walk through floodwaters, follow evacuation instructions, stay away from closed roads and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones if they can do so safely. As of Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District says it has responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. In the Vitalia community, the City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department has installed a 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8:00 p.m. tonight, the fire district said. The pump is moving an estimated 7,000 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce flooding in the neighborhood. Additionally, SLCFD says routine evacuation operations in Vitalia have been suspended overnight and are scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies. Residents experiencing immediate safety or serious medical concerns requiring assistance should call 911.

Even as key Senate races remain unresolved in Mississippi and Alaska, Republicans have already begun searching for someone to blame after a devastating midterm election defeat. With Democrats securing control of the Senate and on track for major gains in the House, the conversation in Washington has quickly shifted from counting ballots to assigning responsibility.The outstanding races remain extraordinarily close. In Mississippi, just over 1,000 votes separate the candidates, with additional mail ballots still eligible to arrive under state law. Alaska's contest may take even longer to resolve because of its ranked-choice voting system, where second- and third-choice preferences could ultimately determine the winner.But while election officials continue tallying votes, Republicans are increasingly focused on what many in the party view as one of the worst electoral setbacks in decades.RELATED STORY | Democratic leaders outline agenda after sweeping Congress in midtermsThe finger-pointing has already begun.One of the first casualties appears to be House Republican leadership. Speaker Mike Johnson has announced he will not seek another term as the party's leader in the House, guaranteeing a new face at the helm as Republicans attempt to regroup.Attention is also turning toward the White House and Trump's inner circle. Vice President JD Vance sparked discussion across Washington after publicly arguing that the party's losses were primarily tied to the conflict with Iran.In a social media post, Vance argued that the war was the central reason for the GOP's defeat and suggested any effort to rebuild the party must begin with an honest assessment of that decision.The comments have intensified scrutiny on senior administration officials, particularly Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Some Republicans are openly questioning whether changes at the Pentagon or elsewhere in the administration are necessary after the election results.The debate echoes a familiar chapter in modern political history. Following Republican losses in the 2006 midterm elections, President George W. Bush replaced Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld amid growing criticism over the Iraq War. Some Republicans are drawing parallels between that election and the party's current predicament.RELATED STORY | DNC chair says Democrats must deliver on promises after midterm winsPresident Donald Trump, however, publicly defended Hegseth this week, telling reporters he believes the defense secretary is doing "a very good job."Still, speculation about Hegseth's future persists. Some Republicans have floated the possibility of a Senate appointment in Tennessee after Sen. Marsha Blackburn won the state's gubernatorial race, creating a vacancy that will need to be filled.Meanwhile, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has emerged as one of the loudest voices calling for a major course correction. DeSantis described the election results as an "extinction event" for Republicans and argued the party must embrace significant changes if it hopes to remain competitive in future national elections.As the final votes are counted and several races remain undecided, Republicans face an uncomfortable reality: the battle over who lost the election may end up lasting longer than the election itself.For now, the GOP's internal reckoning is underway, with leaders, advisers and administration officials all finding themselves under increasing pressure as the party searches for answers after a sweeping Democratic victory.

The City of Boca Raton is expanding its school zone speed camera program to three additional locations beginning Nov. 9.The city said the expansion will add speed cameras in school zones serving Calusa Elementary School, Blue Lake Elementary School, and Omni Middle School/Spanish River High School, bringing the total number of participating school zones in the city to six.Westlake considers school zone speed cameras near Seminole Ridge High School to improve student safetyThe city operates the School Zone Safety Program in partnership with RedSpeed. Cameras are designed to deter speeding and will capture violations only while school zone flashing lights are activated.The new locations and enforcement times are:Calusa Elementary School2051 Clint Moore RoadMorning: 7:05 a.m. to 8:05 a.m.Afternoon: 2 p.m. to 2:35 p.m.Blue Lake Elementary SchoolMilitary Trail and Potomac RoadMorning: 7:20 a.m. to 8:05 a.m.Afternoon: 2 p.m. to 2:35 p.m.Omni Middle School/Spanish River High SchoolJog Road and Yamato RoadMorning: 7 a.m. to 9:35 a.m.Afternoon: 2:45 p.m. to 4:35 p.m.Each school zone will have a 30-day warning period when its cameras are first activated.After the warning period ends, drivers traveling at least 11 mph over the posted speed limit while the school zone lights are flashing can receive a $100 civil penalty.Delray Beach school zone cameras issue nearly 5,000 speeding ticketsMore than 200 drivers ticketed in first week of Boca Raton school zone speed camerasAccording to the city, citations issued through the program do not add points to a driver's license or affect auto insurance rates.Boca Raton previously implemented the program in the school zones for Addison Mizner School, Boca Raton Community High School and J.C. Mitchell Elementary School.For more information, visit their website.

A Greenacres mother says her family lost their home after a deadly Learjet 60 crash Sunday sent flames and burning debris onto their property. Days later, Stephanie Platts told WPTV she is grateful her family escaped but is now turning to the community for help as they try to rebuild.“It was absolute chaos,” Platts said. “There was a lot of fire, a lot of debris, a lot of screaming.”WATCH REPORT BELOW:Platts told WPTV she was home with her family when the jet crashed just yards away.“We didn’t have time to think, we didn’t have time to process it,” Platts said. “The only thing that we had time to do was get to safety.”Platts said she didn't immediately understand what had happened until she encountered the flames.“I didn’t realize that it was an actual explosion until I was faced with flames,” she said.She described large pieces of burning debris hitting the roof of her home as the fire spread.“There were giant chunks of debris that were on fire that pelted my roof,” Platts said.Her home was devastated by the fire, leaving her family displaced. Platts also says she suffered a burn to her foot during the chaos, leaving it swollen. Now, Platts is trying to figure out how her family can move forward and eventually return home.“I want to be able to go back home and enjoy the holidays coming around,” she said.Platts told WPTV that Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach has assisted her while she temporarily stays at the Greenacres Community Center.A GoFundMe has also been set up to support Platts after the crash.Help Stephanie Platts through the GoFundMeEven as she copes with losing her home, Platts said she is thinking about the nine lives lost in the crash just steps from where her family lived.“It’s very heartbreaking for me,” Platts said. “But at the same time, it could have been worse. But every life is important. It doesn’t matter if it was nine or 100, it’s still a life.”Platts said the tragedy has changed how she looks at life.“Life is very short and it can change instantaneously,” she said.Her message to others is simple: “Just embrace it and enjoy it because you don’t know what’s gonna happen tomorrow.”Crews continue to investigate the deadly crash.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

November marks National Veterans and Military Families Month, and WPTV is examining ways to celebrate and support our service members. Former Top Gun pilot Chris Claflin is doing his part and paying it forward to fellow veterans struggling with addiction issues.WATCH REPORT BELOW: After a WPTV Let's Hear It story presented by morning anchor Ashley Glass, a viewer reached out and invited Claflin to speak at the Called to Freedom Veterans Retreat. He happily accepted the invitation. "Serving in the military, no matter what your service is, there’s something about meeting other people who are willing to put their lives on the line for the nation. It was an immediate bond right there," Claflin said. Claflin graduated from Harvard Business School. Navy pilot and flew jets in combat, but all of that success fell apart when he became drug addicted for eight years.Claflin traced the onset of the drug addiction, in part, back to not dealing with trauma he experienced as a child. He is currently more than a year sober, and has a message for anyone struggling, especially veterans. You can’t do this on your own. It's not something you can figure out. Once you get so far down the rabbit hole, you can’t pull yourself out on your own."Claflin has been greatly supported by the Hanley Center in West Palm Beach, a community resource to support the mental health and well-being of service members or anyone struggling.He is currently working to become a certified addiction counselor and aims to have that certificate by spring.

Much of a Jensen Beach neighborhood on Hyline Drive is underwater after this week's heavy rain overwhelmed the local drainage system. As of Wednesday afternoon, water levels inside some homes are still rising long after the rain stopped.For Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid, a kayak has become the way to get around their flooded community.WATCH REPORT BELOW: At Kincaid's home, the water level is waist-deep."We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can," said Kincaid.At French's home, the damage has just begun, with the water level climbing to 4 inches deep."My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else," French said.Their homes are among dozens in the neighborhood under water after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and inundated the drainage system."We were expecting flooding to go down. Clearly drainage is not — things are not draining correctly," Kincaid said.Martin County told us the neighborhood is uniquely located next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other areas that flooded. For now, the county says it's unable to pump water out of the community because the nearby watershed doesn't have capacity, but relief may be on the horizon."As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that," Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said. "We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction."Residents are hoping relief comes sooner rather than later so they can start the long road to recovery."Even after, like, our houses are wrecked," French said."It's just a lot to take in right now for us," Kincaid said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Flooding continues to plague St. Lucie County roads, with officials closing a stretch of South 25th Street near two schools as the district extends school closures through Thursday. Lucie County announced Wednesday that South 25th Street is closed to through traffic between Fort Pierce Central High School at Cobra Pride Way and the entrance to Forest Grove Middle School at Bulldog Drive. County officials said the closure is due to unsafe road conditions caused by flooding. See also: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood The road closure comes as St. Lucie Public Schools announced that schools will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, for another day as the county continues dealing with widespread flooding. Drivers are urged to use caution in the area and find alternate routes. Officials have not announced when the affected stretch of road will reopen. Anyone with questions about the closure can contact the county's Public Works Engineering Division at 772-462-1707 .

Six Palm Beach County schools will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, as the school district continues to assess local conditions affecting its campuses.The closures come after days of heavy rain and flooding across Palm Beach County.The School District of Palm Beach County announced Wednesday evening that the following schools will remain closed Thursday:Egret Lake Elementary SchoolGrassy Waters Elementary SchoolSandpiper Shores Elementary SchoolWashington Elementary SchoolJeaga Middle SchoolWest Boca Raton Community High SchoolAll classes, campus activities and aftercare programs at these schools are canceled Thursday.All other district-operated schools will be open Thursday."Student and staff safety is always our top priority," said Sean Cooley, the district's chief of communications. "The School District of Palm Beach County continues assessing local conditions and the impacts on our campuses. Our goal is to reopen schools as quickly as possible."The district thanked the community for its patience as officials work to safely reopen the affected schools.

Parents and teachers across Palm Beach County are questioning why the School District of Palm Beach County only decided to close some schools after flooding made roads difficult or impossible to navigate countywide.Ten of the district's 182 district-operated schools were closed because of flooding. Nine were announced Wednesday, with a tenth Wednesday morning. The closures stretch from the West Palm Beach area and western communities like Loxahatchee Groves, all the way south to West Boca Raton.But WPTV heard from people across the county asking the same question: Why weren't all schools closed?A WPTV Facebook post informing families about the closures quickly filled with comments from people describing conditions in their own neighborhoods. Some said all schools should have been closed, while others shared pictures of flooded roads outside their homes.One person said they work at a school that remained open but live in an area affected by flooding."I was texting people in the morning trying to figure out if I can leave, even leave my community," said Kim Landis.Landis is a fourth-grade teacher at Coral Sunset Elementary School in Boca Raton and is among those who contacted WPTV for help getting answers from the district. Landis still reported to work, but when asked what her route there was like, she didn't hesitate."Horrible, horrible," Landis said.She described encountering vehicles struggling with the conditions, including a school bus."There were vehicles that were stuck. There's been vehicles stuck since yesterday on the road. It's just, it's horrible," Landis said.Her concern goes beyond the conditions immediately surrounding an individual school. Landis said teachers and students in choice programs may have to commute to schools outside the areas where they live, potentially putting them on roads affected by flooding even if their destination school is open."Why aren't all the districts closed? We have three hurricane days a year that we didn't even get to, we didn't use," Landis said.The district sent a message telling families and staff, "Your personal safety is our top priority," and announced that students who miss class because of flooding will be excused.For employees, however, the policy is different. Educators who cannot make it to work are required to use a sick or personal day."So if I called out, I would have to use my own time, which is not fair," Landis said. "Their top priority is the safety of all staff and students. Well, I'm not so sure about that if we had to come to work today.".WPTV reached out to the school district to ask why it did not close schools districtwide.The district responded with the following statement:"The School District of Palm Beach County prioritizes student and staff safety while striving to keep as many of our 182 schools open as possible. Because Palm Beach County spans more than 2,300 square miles, weather and road conditions vary drastically from one neighborhood to the next. When flooding is localized rather than countywide, we evaluate conditions and make operational decisions on a campus-by-campus basis. This targeted approach prevents unaffected students from losing valuable instructional time.For our educators and staff, personal safety comes first. Any employee unable to travel safely to work should follow our standard leave procedures and may use any available leave (sick, personal, comp, or annual leave). Employees are required to work or submit leave in order to be paid when their primary work location is open.Families unable to safely transport their children to school due to flooded neighborhood streets should contact their school's front office so the student's absence can be excused.There have been no reports of any school district buses getting stuck in water this morning."We thank our families, educators, and staff for their flexibility and cooperation," Sean Cooley, Chief of Communications for the School District of Palm Beach County said in a statement. WPTV also asked why staff members affected by flooding are not being excused in the same way as students. As of the reporting of this story, the district had not responded to that question.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Voters made history Tuesday, electing candidates who will become the first to hold some of the nation’s highest offices.The victories crossed barriers of race, religion, gender and sexual orientation, changing not only which party holds power, but who has historically had the opportunity to hold it.The breakthroughs came as Democrats made broad gains despite the party’s weak standing with the public. A Gallup poll released Oct. 13 found 43% of Americans viewed the Democratic Party favorably, while a majority viewed it unfavorably.Some of the most significant firsts came in governors’ races.In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history.“This win is for all of us,” Bottoms said in her victory speech. “No matter who you voted for tonight, I will be a governor for all of Georgia.”In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor.“Tonight, in our nation's 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected governor in U.S. history,” Haaland said in her victory speech Tuesday.In Texas, which flipped from red to blue, Gina Hinojosa was elected as the state’s first Latina governor, while California elected its first elected Latino governor, Xavier Becerra.A record five Black governors will serve at the same time. Wes Moore in Maryland, Byron Donalds in Florida, Bottoms in Georgia, David Crowley in Wisconsin and Aaron Ford in Nevada will hold their states’ top offices. Moore is currently the nation’s only sitting Black governor, but that will change in January.The Senate delivered another series of firsts. In the battleground state of Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will become the chamber’s first Muslim member, after a campaign in which his identity was frequently attacked by Republicans.“To all the kids who watched this last month, to all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocked someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost,” El-Sayed said.Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate. In her victory speech, she vowed to deliver on lower costs for families, end the Iran war, pass Medicare, and “rip ICE apart.”“We know that people demanded more,” Flanagan said. “And for those of us elected in this moment, it is our duty to deliver.”New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas, who became the first openly gay man elected to US Senate, told voter his win was a victory over the “broken status quo.”“You said in a resounding voice that American needs a course correction; that Washington needs a new generation at the table to fix things,” Pappas said in his speech.With Democrats regaining control of the House, another historic first could come in January. Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the first Black speaker of the House. On Capitol Hill Wednesday, Jeffries told Scripps News, “It was a big night for the American people and a massive repudiation of MAGA extremism. We’re looking forward as House Democrats to getting to work.”

A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago.Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WPTV that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense's second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing held Wednesday.Camerlengo's attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense's amended motion was "procedurally invalid and facially insufficient."Wednesday's ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set.Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care.Her arrest followed a WPTV investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade.The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case.During a contentious July hearing, Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo's defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial."I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do," Metzger said. "This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count."In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027.That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial.Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths."I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts," Kaplan previously told WPTV.Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022.Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako's death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive.Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo's arrest."I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn't think it would be two years," Kirk Csontos previously told WPTV.Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful."I'm still hopeful. Believe it or not, I'm still hopeful that she will be held accountable," she said.Camerlengo's next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. 1.No trial date has been announced.

WPTV hasn't stopped looking into the tragic death of a Port St. Lucie teen who was killed while walking to school just last month.On Wednesday, WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield sat down with the family for the first time to hear from them about their son and the questions they're still asking.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jacory Brown, a freshman at Treasure Coast High School, was struck and killed by a car on Port St. Lucie Boulevard while walking to school early in the morning on Oct. 7."He just went to school," Shelly-Ann Findley-Brown, mother, said. "He was supposed to come back home. His birthday would be on Monday. He would have been 15."Findley-Brown, father Ainsworth Brown and grandfather Clovis Brown, sat down with WPTV.They're remembering Jacory’s smile."He's kind, he's a jovial kid,” said Findley-Brown. "He's the life of our party of five." They’re remembering his friendliness to others."[He] was loved by so many persons, and he has touched everybody he's met," Finely-Brown said. And they're remembering his passion for entrepreneurship and graphic design — like making cover art, business cards and flyers for friends and family."His hand was always up here, mind looking, his eyes all over like he's devising a plan and coming up with his thing," Findley-Brown said. But the family still has questions.They say Port St. Lucie Boulevard, with all the construction, makes it a dangerous roadway for kids walking to school."The road conditions are horrible," Findley-Brown said. "You are walking in puddles. And the night before, it rained. There was water all over the place. There's literally no sidewalks for kids to walk."FDOT started construction back in 2025 to widen the road from two to four lanes and add new sidewalks and lights.But the project isn't expected to be completed until winter 2028."I hope the state takes this into a big consideration because it's not right walking to school when you don't have proper sidewalks," Findley-Brown said.Jacory Brown will be laid to rest on Nov. 14.Friends have started a GoFundMe to support the family.

The election night victory for Amendment 3 in Florida now sets up property tax savings for homeowners with the state's homestead exemption."No one who has homestead today in the state of Florida needs to worry about calling us or coming in or doing anything at this point," said Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Those homeowners, she said, will automatically see their exemption rise to $150,000 in the first notices going out in August 2027."It's important they know that they aren't going to see those savings until the end of 2027," Jacks said.Tax bills, which are not being eliminated, are sent out in November by the county's tax collector."Everyone will continue to pay the school board," Jacks said. "In addition, any non-ad valorem assessments, so assessments based usually on fees, the most common one is the solid waste authority, those won't go away."Homeowners who have established Florida residency and apply by Dec. 31 are eligible for the new exemption.New Florida residents in 2027 will have to wait five years for the higher exemption.And renters established in the state by Dec. 31 will be eligible for the higher exemption if they buy a home in the future.For cities and counties in Florida, the future looks uncertain as tax revenues will decrease.Many local government leaders have speculated they will need to turn to budget trimming, cutting services and possibly looking for other revenue streams."The first decision they're going to have to make is how do they protect, or if they protect, police and fire," said former state Sen. Ron DeSantis, a supporter of Amendment 3, has said he'll call a special session to work out the details of handling Amendment 3."I think the first thing they need to do is be honest about what this means for counties and cities," Brandes said. "They have to protect the counties. They do not need to protect or have to protect the cities, and frankly, there's gonna be some cities that fail, and they need to let them fail."

Change is on the horizon in Washington.Democrats swept both the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections, positioning the party to take control of Congress in January for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.“The days of the House of Representatives functioning as a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Wednesday. The New York Democrat is widely expected to succeed Republican Mike Johnson as House speaker in January.RELATED STORY | Vance blames Iran war for sweeping Republican midterm lossesJeffries spoke exclusively with Scripps News Chief Washington Correspondent Joe St. George, indicating he would consider cutting deals with President Donald Trump when they can find common ground. “In this Congress, Democrats came together with our Republican colleagues in the House and in the Senate to pass a housing affordability bill, because we know we have to build more housing that the American people can afford," he said. "That may hopefully provide a foundation for the type of work that can be done together with our Republican colleagues in order to bring about the type of meaningful change the American people demanded.”Democrats have also vowed to address what voters across the country cited as top concerns: high costs, the ongoing war in Iran and cracking down on corruption.RELATED STORY | 2026 midterm election results: Key races for Senate, House and governorIn a post on X, congressional Democrats on the Oversight Committee listed some of their top targets. Among them: corporations ripping off Americans, administration officials accused of profiting off the presidency, and associates of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.With control of the Senate, Democrats will have the power to confirm or reject President Donald Trump's nominees for Cabinet positions and other high-level administration posts. They will also control the confirmation process for federal judges, including any future nominees to the U.S. Supreme Court.Asked how Democrats would handle Trump's nominees, Sen. Chuck Schumer, who is expected to become Senate majority leader in January, signaled that his party would closely scrutinize the president's picks.“We want judicial nominees, like we showed in ‘23 and ‘24, who obey the law, who have fidelity to the rule of law," he said. "Too many of Trump’s nominees did not have that at all."

It's a new season for the FAU Owls basketball team, with a lot of new faces, including the school's highest-rated recruit in school history, Felipe Quinones."I'm just grateful to play at a level I could only dream of playing at," said Quinones, a 6-foot-4, four-star recruit who impresses in transition and can simply put the ball in the basket.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "It's a dream come true, and I'm living my dream right now, so it's easy and fun. Lucie homeowners whose properties were damaged by this week's flooding could be eligible for up to $25,000 in financial assistance for critical repairs.The city announced Wednesday that it has allocated $1 million to its Disaster Relief Program to help low- and moderate-income homeowners repair their primary residences.WATCH REPORT: Heavy rain floods Port St. LuciePre-applications for the program will open at 8 a.m. 5, and funding will remain available until the $1 million allocation is exhausted.The assistance is being offered through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding provided by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation.Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000 through a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years in accordance with program guidelines.According to the city, the money may be used for emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable.Eligible expenses may include:Tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitabilityPayment of Homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation workTemporary repairs to prevent further property damage, such as:Roof repairsWeatherproofingWater extractionRemoval of water-damaged materialsEmergency plumbing or electrical workTemporary structural stabilization Other reasonable and necessary actions required to protect the home from additional damageAll work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided.The program does not cover mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal or remediation. If a home requires mold remediation, the homeowner must have that work completed before other approved repairs can proceed.Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded.To be eligible, applicants must meet the program's income requirements.They must also have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home must have an assessed value of $560,154 or less, and applicants must be current on their mortgage and property tax payments.The city's pre-application process opens at 8 a.m. Thursday.Residents can apply through the city's housing website.Homeowners who need assistance can also contact Port St. Lucie's Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.Because the city has allocated a limited $1 million pool of funding, the program will remain open only until those funds are exhausted.

As floodwaters slowly recede across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, homeowners are facing a costly question: Who pays for flood damage if they don't have flood insurance?More than a foot of rain inundated some neighborhoods across the region this week, flooding homes, stranding drivers and forcing some residents to evacuate.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Among the hardest-hit areas was the Ibis neighborhood in West Palm Beach, where floodwaters left dozens of vehicles stranded and streets submerged.But despite the widespread flooding, much of the neighborhood sits outside federally designated high-risk flood zones, leaving some residents without flood insurance.One Ibis resident, Lee, watched as heavy rain transformed her neighborhood into what looked more like a lake."It was coming down so hard that you couldn't see the ground," she said. Lee described the scene as "apocalyptic," recalling the shock of seeing cars stranded in floodwaters."I was overwhelmed by this whole thing — walking and seeing people's cars stranded in the middle," she said.Like many homeowners who live outside high-risk flood zones, Lee never thought she would need flood insurance."Who thought? We moved west so we didn't have to get the flood insurance," she said.According to insurance attorney Aaron Bass, homeowners who don't have separate flood insurance generally cannot rely on their standard homeowners policies to cover damage caused by rising floodwaters."There's no loopholes to get flood coverage from your regular homeowner's insurance policy, Kate. It just doesn't exist," Bass said.That means homeowners without flood insurance could be responsible for thousands — or even hundreds of thousands — of dollars in repairs.However, Bass said there are other resources worth exploring.Bass recommends contacting the Federal Emergency Management Agency and nonprofit disaster relief organizations to see what assistance may be available."You're going to have to call FEMA, see if they're going to help you, and you need to call nongovernmental organizations, charities," Bass said.FEMA assistance is not guaranteed. Eligibility depends on several factors, including whether federal disaster assistance has been authorized for the affected area.Some disaster assistance may also be available through low-interest loans, which must be repaid.Yet nonprofit organizations can provide another avenue for help.Jacob Rutz, senior program manager with Samaritan's Purse, said the organization has teams in areas of the southeast helping disaster victims with recovery efforts."Our volunteer teams work on roofs, tarping them, stopping water from coming in," Rutz said.The organization is among several nonprofits that help homeowners recover from disasters, particularly when insurance payments or other assistance are delayed or unavailable.Rutz encourages residents to start by checking with local emergency management agencies to find out what resources are available."The most important thing really is to look at your local emergency services website," he said.He recommended residents also call 211 to connect with local community assistance programs.Bass said the flooding serves as a reminder that living outside a designated high-risk flood zone does not eliminate the risk of flooding.His recommendation? Consider purchasing flood insurance even if your mortgage lender doesn't require it."That $300, $400, $500 a year for a premium for a federal flood insurance policy is small potatoes compared to hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage to your home," Bass said.Actual flood insurance premiums vary depending on the property, location and coverage selected.For homeowners already dealing with damage, experts recommend documenting everything with photos and videos, keeping receipts and contacting local emergency management officials about available assistance.Meanwhile, Lee is finding a little humor in her neighborhood's unexpected waterfront transformation.Her next investment?"I'm going to invest in one of those roll-up boats," she laughed. "So we can get around!"Residents affected by flooding can explore the following resources:FEMA: Visit DisasterAssistance.gov to check whether federal disaster assistance is available in your area.Samaritan's Purse: Visit SamaritansPurse.org for information about disaster relief efforts.211: Dial 211 or visit 211.org to connect with local nonprofit and community resources.U.S. Small Business Administration: Visit SBA.gov for information about disaster loans, which may be available to eligible homeowners and renters, not just business owners.Flood insurance: Visit FloodSmart.gov to learn about flood coverage through the National Flood Insurance Program.Palm Beach County: Visit the County's Individual Disaster and Family Assistance site. St Lucie County: Visit the County's Emergency Preparedness Portal, and scroll to "Report Damage" and/or "After the Emergency" Indian River County: Visit the Emergency Management site for disaster grants, loans, and insurance informationMartin County: Visit the County's Disaster Recovery page for information on insurance, building permits, damage assessment and more. Okeechobee County: Visit the Emergency Homepage for important links to resources like the Red Cross, FEMA Disaster Assistance, and Emergency Contacts.

A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street Gang has led to a law enforcement operation in St. Lucie County, the sheriff’s office said. Officials are expected to discuss the operation, criminal charges and the group’s alleged involvement in violent crimes and drug trafficking at a news conference Thursday. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. The sheriff’s office did not provide details about arrests or charges in its release. Officials scheduled a news conference for 2:30 p.m. Thursday at sheriff’s office headquarters. Sheriff Richard Del Toro , Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith and representatives from participating agencies are expected to speak. CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized. The sheriff’s office said Thursday’s briefing will provide further details about the investigation and enforcement operation. CBS12 News will provide updates from the news conference later today.

A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago. Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WFLX that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. Camerlengo’s attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.” Wednesday’s ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set. Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Her arrest followed a WFLX investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade. The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case. During a contentious July hearing , Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial. “I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I’ve lost count.” In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial. Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths. “I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don’t think she had all of the facts,” Kaplan previously told WFLX. Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako’s death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo’s arrest. “I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn’t think it would be two years,” Kirk Csontos previously told WFLX. Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful. Believe it or not, I’m still hopeful that she will be held accountable,” she said. Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. No trial date has been announced.

Lucie Public Schools will remain closed Thursday as the county continues to recover from flooding caused by this week's severe weather.The school district announced Wednesday that campuses will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, because of ongoing road conditions, including numerous flooded bus stops and areas where high water remains.WATCH REPORT BELOW: District officials said they want to allow additional time for the flooding to subside before returning to normal operations.Essential employees are required to report to work as outlined in the district's Emergency Operations Plan.Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district cautioned that could change depending on conditions.Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen."Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event," the district said.

Palm Beach County Fire Rescue crews rescued and evacuated several people during three days of widespread flooding that left vehicles stranded, roads impassable and some neighborhoods covered by several feet of water.The department said its flood response operations began Sunday and continued through Tuesday as crews responded to emergencies in several parts of the county.WATCH BELOW: Aerial video of flooding in Century VillageOne of the largest operations unfolded Sunday evening in the Century Village area of unincorporated central Palm Beach County.Beginning around 5 p.m., firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls from the area. Nearly 100 residents were trapped in stranded vehicles as water rose rapidly, according to PBCFR.Firefighters reported encountering cars floating with people still inside and water reaching 3 to 4 feet deep in some locations.To help locate people in need of rescue, PBCFR deployed drones over Century Village, Cypress Lakes the Tennis Club and surrounding areas. The drones flew around stranded vehicles and used thermal-imaging cameras to search for people.Using information gathered from the air, firefighters waded through floodwater and deployed high-water vehicles and brush trucks to reach residents and bring them to higher ground.Despite the dangerous conditions, PBCFR said no injuries were reported during those rescues.WATCH BELOW: Aerial video of flooding, rescues in Riviera BeachThe response continued Monday night when PBCFR's Urban Search and Rescue Swiftwater Response Team deployed to flooded neighborhoods in Riviera Beach.The team remained in the area for nearly 24 hours, deploying emergency rafts and boats and going door to door to check on residents where flooded streets had become impassable to normal vehicles.During that operation, PBCFR said crews evacuated 71 people, conducted two medical rescues and evacuated nine pets.The flood response came as the department was also dedicating dozens of personnel and other resources to the aircraft crash site along Military Trail, including a mobile command post.Overall, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue said it responded to more than 1,600 emergency calls countywide during the three-day period after the flooding began.That figure includes all 911 calls handled by the department, not just flooding-related emergencies.

WPTV Westlake reporter Christy Waite checked out a new family-owned eye care practice, bringing another healthcare option closer to home for residents of the growing city.Dr. Tuyet-Suong Pham and her husband recently opened Westlake Eye Care, a practice they built from the ground up. The office offers routine eye exams and diagnoses and treats eye diseases.WATCH BELOW: New eye care practice opens in WestlakePham said opening her own practice has been a longtime dream, but she also wanted to provide families in Westlake with care closer to home."I wanted to provide quality care to the families here so they can get the care they need closer to home," Pham said.Since opening their doors this fall, the couple said they are already seeing their business grow."Over the past two months we have seen a couple hundred patients, and we are accepting new ones," Pham said.Patient Jeff Cap said having an eye doctor nearby means he no longer has to travel as far for care.“Oh! It’s so awesome because I don’t have to drive 30-40 minutes. It’s just right around the corner,” Cap said.As more patients come through the doors, Pham said another trend is catching her eye: nearsightedness in children."It is projected that by the year 2050 that 50% of the population will be nearsighted," Pham said.Pham said screen time can play a role, while children are also spending less time outdoors. She is urging parents to make sure their children have their eyes checked, particularly as nearsightedness becomes more common among kids.She said nearsightedness can increase the risk of serious eye complications later in life, including retinal detachment, glaucoma and macular degeneration, and other serious conditions.As Westlake continues to grow, some residents say they would also like to see more medical services grow with it. Cap said he would like to see the existing emergency room eventually expand into a full-scale hospital."I would like to see the ER expand. They are open Monday and Tuesday 8:30 a.m. and Wednesday and Thursday 9:30 a.m. They are closed Fridays and Sundays but are open on Saturdays 9:30 am- to 3:30 p.m.

The Miami Dolphins returned to practice Wednesday after a 24-19 loss to the New England Patriots on Sunday, with head coach Jeff Hafley emphasizing growth and development over results at the midpoint of the NFL regular season. Going into Week 9, the rebuilding Dolphins sit in last place in the AFC East Division with a 1-6 record.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "While disappointed being 1-6, it's not, it's bigger than the result. It's about the process; it's about the constant quest to be better today than we were yesterday," Hafley said.Hafley is sticking with the same focus he has had all season: growth and development. He says he likes how the Dolphins are playing with intensity and aggressiveness."That's how we are playing football. I mean, I think if you watch us right now, and I think every coach has said it, and everybody who watches us, whether it's on TV or they turn on our tape, I get texts or phone calls that's what showing up on tape right now and while it's disappointing that we're 1-6, the foundation of that with young guys, that's really important to us," Hafley said. "When you see the physicality and the toughness and how hard guys are playing, it means that they're playing for each other and that they're bought in and that we've brought the right guys here."When asked about the Dolphins receivers, Hafley pointed to guys like Malik Washington, Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, Kevin Coleman and Jalen Tolbert as a group he's excited about."You take a group like that, and there needs to be constant improvement and development. They just haven't played very much. It's new, you know, it's a new league for them. There's a bright future there. They just have to continue to work really hard. And that starts today again in practice. But I am excited about that group," Hafley said.Sunday will be Game 8 for Miami, as the team faces the Detroit Lions — a squad Hafley says has the best offense in the league."It is going to be a challenge, and I view that as a challenge that we look forward to. I mean, anytime you get a chance to go up against the top offense in the league, you need to prepare and you need to rise up to the level that you're going to play against. And for a young group of guys, I mean, I think it's really exciting. It's a great opportunity for us," Hafley said.The matchup against the Lions is at home on Sunday. The Dolphins still have not won at Hard Rock Stadium this year, and this could be the week they give the home crowd a win.

Local food makers, artists and community organizations are getting a new waterfront showcase in Jupiter as Charlie & Joe's at Love Street launches a series of events designed to support local vendors and bring families together.The first Heart & Harvest market is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. at Love Street in Jupiter.Lucky Shuck Executive Chef John Daly told WPTV the event is focused on supporting the people who live and work in the community."It's all about supporting local, our local vendors, our local fishermen," Daly said during WPTV’s Shining A Light. Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways?ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now,” Jessop said.Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study.Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating.“They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas,” she said.The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released.Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment.“Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations,” Shanker said.The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations.Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10.A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project.“My students are creating drift cards which they will be releasing on November 10 here at Manatee Lagoon, and they are doing this to track the pollution in the waterways and apply what we're learning in the classroom to the real world,” she said.And the students aren't sending anonymous pieces of orange material into the water.They're making the cards their own.One student decorated a card with water, a sun and a shark, before adding a marine-themed message: “You're 'fintastic.'”Another decorated a card as an ocean scene with a simple message for whoever eventually discovers it: “Love your ocean.”For students, the cards turn an environmental lesson into something tangible.They create the cards, release them, and wait to see where currents carry them. If members of the public find and report their locations, those discoveries become part of the study.That provides a real-world demonstration of something that can otherwise be difficult to visualize in a classroom: What happens to floating material after it enters a waterway?For the broader community, it also turns a walk along the water into an opportunity to participate in local science.If you spot one of the bright orange drift cards, it may be more than something that washed ashore. Its location is precisely the information researchers are looking for.The experiment comes just before another important date for the Lake Worth Lagoon.Manatee season officially begins Nov. 15.Shanker said cooler temperatures help bring manatees back toward Manatee Lagoon.“As the water temperatures drop, they start coming here to Manatee Lagoon for our warm water outflow,” Shanker said.Manatee Lagoon plans to celebrate the beginning of the season with a kickoff event Nov. 21.For the students creating drift cards, meanwhile, the next milestone comes Nov. 10, when their colorful creations leave their hands and begin their journey through South Florida's waterways.Where they end up is part of the experiment.Who finds them could be anyone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. One man was killed, and two others were critically injured on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said.The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down late Wednesday morning near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, while on a trip to film boats on the water, the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during an afternoon news conference that the two survivors were taken to a nearby trauma center in critical but stable condition.Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.When the sheriff's office marine patrol units reached the scene, they reported finding a Good Samaritan trying to help one of the victims and take him to shore. Miami firefighters attempted to save his life, but he didn't survive, Cordero-Stutz said.Meanwhile, border protection officers found the two other men from the helicopter and turned them over to Miami-Dade rescue workers for transport to the hospital.Cordero-Stutz said the cause of the crash remains under investigation. South Florida has experienced heavy showers over the past few days, but it wasn't known if the weather contributed to the crash.Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.Officials didn't immediately identify the helicopter's occupants. The sheriff said they were still working to notify family members.On Sunday, nine people died when a Learjet plummeted into the ground near West Palm Beach, Florida, with enough force to create a crater and pulverize the airplane. The NTSB is also investigating that crash.

Much of a Jensen Beach neighborhood on Hyline Drive is underwater after this week's heavy rain overwhelmed the local drainage system. As of Wednesday afternoon, water levels inside some homes are still rising long after the rain stopped.For Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid, a kayak has become the way to get around their flooded community.WATCH REPORT BELOW: At Kincaid's home, the water level is waist-deep."We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can," said Kincaid.At French's home, the damage has just begun, with the water level climbing to 4 inches deep."My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else," French said.Their homes are among dozens in the neighborhood under water after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and inundated the drainage system."We were expecting flooding to go down. Clearly drainage is not — things are not draining correctly," Kincaid said.Martin County told us the neighborhood is uniquely located next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other areas that flooded. For now, the county says it's unable to pump water out of the community because the nearby watershed doesn't have capacity, but relief may be on the horizon."As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that," Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said. "We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction."Residents are hoping relief comes sooner rather than later so they can start the long road to recovery."Even after, like, our houses are wrecked," French said."It's just a lot to take in right now for us," Kincaid said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Jensen Beach mother says floodwaters forced her family out of their home and left her street impassable. Lisa French, who lives on NE Cheri Drive, told CBS12 News in an email that her family, including her two young children, had to evacuate as the water kept rising. She said several neighbors have more than three feet of water inside their homes and that the water kept rising even after the heavy rain stopped. French said she used a kayak to get a stranded UPS driver out of the neighborhood and to bring food to neighbors who could not leave. The entire neighborhood has been helping one another, but families are losing their homes and belongings, French wrote. Lucie recovery efforts continue after record-breaking floods French said many homeowners in her neighborhood do not have flood insurance because residents never thought of it as a flood-prone area. Martin County’s flood protection page warns that the typical homeowner’s insurance policy does not include coverage for damage resulting from flooding, and that there have been multiple instances of homeowners in low- to moderate-risk flood zones (Flood Zone X) who have experienced significant flooding The flooding follows days of heavy rain across the Treasure Coast. On Sunday, the National Weather Service said radar indicated between 2.5 and 4 inches of rain had already fallen by 3:52 p.m. in Martin County and southeastern St. Lucie County, and listed Jensen Beach among the affected communities. Ron DeSantis signed Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency in Martin County and six other counties. The order says a broad area of low pressure brought widespread heavy rainfall across parts of Florida from Oct. Martin County Public Schools closed Tuesday, and the Martin County Supervisor of Elections moved Precinct 2 in Jensen Beach due to flooding for Election Day.

Christia Li Roberts defeated Cherie White for the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat in the Nov. With 60.14% of the vote, Roberts came out victorious against White, who came away with 39.86% of the vote. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. The district includes Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

A fatal crash involving a semi-truck and a vehicle has shut down Warfield Boulevard in Indiantown, prompting a response from multiple agencies. Martin County Sheriff’s deputies, Martin County Fire Rescue, and Florida Highway Patrol have responded to the crash, which occurred on Warfield Boulevard just north of Fox Brown Road. Warfield Boulevard is closed to through traffic between Fox Brown Road and Martin Highway. The closure is expected to last several hours while Florida Highway Patrol investigates. Anyone needing to reach an address on Warfield Boulevard between Martin Highway and Fox Brown Road must travel south from Martin Highway.
